name: LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator), Sandia National Laboratories
origin_detail: Began in the mid-1990s under a CRADA between two DOE labs (Sandia and LLNL) and three companies (Cray, Bristol-Myers Squibb, DuPont); coding led by Steve Plimpton at Sandia. Fortran LAMMPS 99 and LAMMPS 2001 followed; the C++ rewrite was first released as open source on 1 September 2004.
openness_notes: A 2025 case study by the developers says LAMMPS 99 was 'available under a no-cost license, but was not open source'; the LAMMPS 99 documentation, by contrast, described it as GPL, so the initial level is uncertain. Since the 2004 C++ release LAMMPS is GPLv2. Development is led by a Sandia-anchored team (12 core developers at five US and European institutions in 2025) rather than a foundation, so it scores 3.

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Code grew from ~50,000 lines in 2004 to >1.32 million lines and 430+ contributors by May 2025.

risk_events: No long-term-support releases 'due to limited workforce and funding' (developers, 2025).
Expected leadership transition as senior developers retire; maintenance earns little academic credit.
Testing infrastructure partly depends on a Temple University cluster that could become unavailable.
robustness: GPLv2 code on GitHub with 430+ contributors and 92 optional packages; core team spread over five institutions; packaged by Linux distributions. Active cadence (stable release 30 Sep 2026, feature release 13 Nov 2026, ~7,400 commits between stable releases). Core funding still flows mainly from DOE through Sandia.
physical_science_relevance: One of the standard open classical MD engines for materials science, chemistry and soft matter; the main host for running machine-learned interatomic potentials at scale on DOE supercomputers. R&D 100 award 2018.
openness_effect_assessment: Opening the code under the GPL in 2004 turned a lab-internal CRADA code into a community platform: hundreds of outside contributors added physics packages, and the code grew ~25-fold in size. The trade-off is maintenance strain: the developers report that features are rewarded but upkeep is not, and that funding does not cover long-term-support releases.
key_takeaway: LAMMPS shows a national-lab code outliving the industrial CRADA that created it by opening up: 30 years on it is a GPL community platform and a default MD engine for ML potentials, with no revenue model. Its fragility is people, not licence: a small DOE-funded core team carries maintenance for a very large user base.
